utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me remind you once again - good morning - that you made a declaration at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth and that you are still bound by that declaration. Understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How much longer are you going to be Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Very brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I'm sure you will be relieved to know that I have just a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're a very pleasant person to talk to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sure. Before I move on to another topic, just a few more details I wanted to ask you about. You would agree, sir, that the attack on Saborsko was originally scheduled to occur on the 10th of November, 1991, but that it was delayed until the 12th of November because of bad weather; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you must have received your order to participate in the attack no later than the 9th of November; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty, but definitely to place several hours ahead of the first planned attack which took place on the morning of the 10th. Therefore, I mean in the afternoon on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So on the -- you received the -- you would agree that you received the order on the 9th of November?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, the -- the three men that were killed at Glibodol Cross, they were killed, you say, on the 8th of November, 1991, but in fact their bodies were not dug out until the 9th, the morning of the 9th of November, 1991. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you. I think that the bodies were dug out on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's -- sir, let's look --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's look, please, at Exhibit 605, which is the report of Dusan Latas, which was written on the 23rd of November. So just 11 days or so after these events. And -- I think -- I think you have the English up on the B/C/S screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've got English, not B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's right. There's English on both at the moment. That's still the English. I wonder if I could inquire of Defence counsel if they have a copy of this exhibit in B/C/S. I do not have a hard copy of it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ah, here we go. It's on. And if we could zoom in on the second half of the page. And this is the second half of the page in English to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It says "On the 8th of November, 1991, our unit was given the task to retake the Glibodol Cross", and then he describes all the things that were done, "searched the sector around Licka Jasenica barracks" and railroad tracks were searched in the morning and then headed toward Glibodol Cross. They go through a minefield. "And then further searches of the road area uncovered our colleague Bogdan Petrovic's vehicle as well as the tractor and trailer belonging to his neighbours. It was immediately obvious that they had been ambushed."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it on my screen, the part that you've been reading out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I think we need to turn to the next page in B/C/S. And if we could turn to the next page in English as well. And if you could just read there, do you see that the scene is found, and there's some digging starts. This is still on the 8th. "We continued digging and found a man's leg under the horse but might fell and we had to cease digging. We waited" -- "we received" -- at the end of the paragraph it says, "We received reinforced security and waited for dawn. The next day," so the 9th of November, 1991, "we extracted two dead horses from the earth pile and then the bodies of the three men were found." Do you see that, sir? And in fact that's how it was, wasn't it? The bodies were dug out on the 9th of November, 1991, as is described in detail in this report.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a detailed description of it here. However, there was an exhibit, an official note, a wartime logbook of TG-2 was presented to me and I believe that there is a report concerning the scene there. I don't recall, but I believe that before I received the order for the attack on Saborsko, I had in my pocket the photographs from the scene. Don't ask me about the time, but I know that it was either on the 7th, 8th or 9th, but you have an exhibit wherein this particular detail is stated, and the report was made on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, the exhibit -- the exhibit that you're referring to, it's Exhibit 108 in evidence. It's the operational report of Tactical Group 2, and all it says is that these men were killed on either the 7th or the 8th of November, 1991. It doesn't say anything about when the bodies were uncovered or anything.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but somewhere to the side the time is stated when this was reported. You have the time and the place of the Official Note, when it was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, we can look at -- there actually is no time there. It just states the date that it occurred and the date, and that's all that's noted there. Sir, in fact the truth is, isn't it, that the -- you -- you never believed for a moment -- you -- or let's put it this way: You knew, even on the 9th of November, 1991, that -- you knew even then that the order -- that the decision to attack Saborsko had been made before those bodies were found. Isn't that true? You knew that on the 9th, you knew that on the 13th, and you knew that on Monday when you testified here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, sir. When I received the order for the attack, I had three Polaroid photos in the pocket of my overalls, and I showed them to others rather selectively, because I knew that it wasn't a good thing to incite anger --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in others, but I hope I will be able to track down these photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, those Polaroids -- if you received the order on the 9th of November, those Polaroids could have only be taken on the 9th of November, 1991, and you could not have believed that an order to -- that a decision to attack Saborsko had been made within the JNA, that it had been passed down and that you had received it all in a matters of hours. You could not have believed that all happened in a matter of hours, sir. You knew that that decision had been made before the bodies were found. Isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm intervening because I don't see the point of the question. I don't see it, and I wonder how the witness will. We have led written evidence showing precisely when and why the decision was taken. It has nothing to do with Glibodol Kriz. I don't know whether my learned friend is trying to test the credibility of the witness or the reason for the attack or something else, but then he should put a direct question stating his case. We have already lost and wasted an hour discussing the link between the attack on Saborsko and Glibodol Kriz. The witness has spent half of the time yesterday talking about the fact that his comment on Glibodol Kriz was his comment alone and had nothing to do with the order. Besides, we -- the witness has been pointing and referring the Prosecutor to TG-2 report item 13, and I believe the Prosecutor should at least take the time to take -- to look at item 13 before proceeding. And I really don't see the point, and I don't see what the Prosecutor is trying to elicit from the witness through these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the objection comes as quite a surprise to me I have to say because if counsel is so clear and he thinks it's so clear that the decision to attack Saborsko was made before the killings at Glibodol Kriz, then I'm a little at a loss as to why counsel allowed the witness to testify on Monday to the opposite, which is -- he said on Monday before the order these events at Glibodol Kriz occurred. Now, when -- when on cross-examination the witness was confronted with the fact that in fact the decision had been made before the murders, the version we got was, well, I received the order before -- I received the order after those killings occurred. And what I'm trying to establish now is that that's false and that is not true. So I -- and finally, Your Honour, it is the witness in his letter which he has adopted, which he wrote on the 13th of November, 1991, it is the witness who said on the 13th of November and said it again in this courtroom on Monday that the -- well, on the 13th he said the immediate cause for the attack was the killings, and on Monday he said before the order -- order was made -- before the order to attack Saborsko the killings occurred. So it is the witness who has linked the two things. I'm simply trying to show that he knew already on the 9th of November that those two things were not connected. I think it's a fair line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any response directly to what the Prosecution has just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecutor is aware of the document. The document is in evidence. This is the decision setting up Tactical Group 2 issued on the 23rd of October, 1991. He also knows that pursuant to this decision TG-2 is tasked with the Plaski area and all its units for the implementation of certain tasks. This took place on the 23rd of October, and the decision was issued by the 5th district -- military district pursuant to an order from the SSNO. The Tactical Group was not set up just merely to march about but to carry out a mission. The other document which is in evidence is the decision setting up Tactical Group 2 issued by the command of the 13th Corps, dated 7 November, 1991. Then the decision issued by Commander Bulat. This is the chronological order that can be found in these military documents, and my learned friend yesterday put to this witness a text which is 1251 or Exhibit 52, and the Prosecutor read out the text himself. The forces of MUP and ZNG have been entrenching themselves in Saborsko, Kusan for some time now, and it is estimated that the -- their strength stands at 400 Ustasha. So that's the reason why the deployment of the MUP and ZNG forces and there is no logic that can indicate the opposite, not even these witness's testimony. What happened at Glibodol Kriz is an incident which has to do with all of this and with witness's conduct as the witness himself explained. Thirdly, Your Honour, the learned friend showed item 11 of the order on the security of the operation, which stated that any unknown person which happens to be in the area of combat should be taken to the command, but what he didn't read was item 1, and that was -- the purpose of it was to preserve the secrecy of the operation and the witness himself stated that he received the order for the attack several hours ahead of the attack. But we cannot leave aside all the written evidence we have and base our case merely on what this witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the one sentence this witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You addressed yourself to the points the Prosecution made. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, I'm going to put my question to you again. You knew, if you received the order only on the afternoon of the 9th of November, 1991, you knew that those bodies had not been dug up and photographed until the morning of the 9th of November, 1991, and you must have known that that order for the attack of Saborsko could not have been, therefore, a result of the discovery of those bodies. You knew that on the 9th of November, 1991, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot agree with you at all. I asked you to show me the document that was drafted at the time of these events that I was already shown. Now you show me the document which was drafted some 10 to 12 days later on and was written from memory. Latas came at the time but he was unable to take notes because we spent together three days in the action of defending the Licka Jasenica barracks. You are trying to persuade me into something --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get the truth, sir. I'm really just trying to get the truth. If you want to look at that document, it's Exhibit 108. We can look at it. If we can go to page 3 of the English, and we're looking for entry 13. It's either on page -- I'm not sure on the B/C/S, whether it's 3 or 4.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we could start --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, let's -- we'll look at the entry you were talking about. Could we look at page 3. It's entry --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It starts from item 3. Could you just lift it up a bit. I'd like to see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Here we go. This is it. Look at number 13. It's the top half of this page. If we could zoom in, please. Do you see there for the entry it says -- for number 13 it says Glibodol Kriz, and the date, it's 7/8 November, 1991. It says on the 7th or 8th of November, 1991, in the region of Glibodol Kriz --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 7th and the 8th. So the night between the 7th and the 8th is what it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It says the three members of the TO of Plaski were killed and it gives their names. You see, sir, there is nothing there which says when the bodies were dug out or when the information was learned. It only says when they were killed. And it was known when they were killed because the scene was found on the 8th of November, 1991. So there is nothing here which contradicts the report of Dusan Latas. Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I indicated that in the left-most column there is the time of the entry when it was written probably by the duty officer, and the duty officer says it happened between the 7th and the 8th, but it is highly likely that the scene had been photographed on the 8th. I'm not sure. I told the Trial Chamber that there was this Polaroid camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not allowing me to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why don't you let me explain what this is about?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want you to answer my questions and I want you to look at something, please. Look at the entry for -- the entry for number 12, please. When was that -- what's the date and time of that, number 12?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th of November, 8.10.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So entry number 13 must have been written after the 9th of November, 0810 hours; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please go back to the beginning of it --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which chronologically states when the attack commenced, because you are pulling things out of their context. Would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- take us back to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- entry 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because again you're asking me to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, would you please answer my question. Entry 13 is after entry 12 and the date and time for entry 12 is the 9th of November -- the 9th of November at 0810 hours. So entry 13 must have been written after that, sometime after -- actually, it's quite clear that it was written between 0810 hours and 1000 hours because entry 14 is 10 o'clock on the 9th of November. So you would agree with me wouldn't you that entry 13 is written between 8.10 in the morning on the 9th of November, and 10.00 in the morning on the 9th of November. Right, sir? If you could answer that question, we could move on. I don't really want to get bogged down on this topic, but I do want answers to the questions.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This time I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we go back to entry 3 where the attack is mentioned for the first time, and there you can see chronologically how the order unfolded, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- all of this took place --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that was written here after the attack on Licka Jasenica. Perhaps then the Defence counsel will put the question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir. If Defence counsel wants to raise anything that he thinks is important, he will have an opportunity to do so. It's not of interest to me at this moment. I'm going to ask you one last question about this, sir, one last before I move on. And that is that the truth of the matter, sir, is that in your letter that you wrote on the 13th of November, 1991, and in court here today, what you have tried to do is use the death of those three men and the circumstances of their death to justify the evil that occurred at Saborsko. Isn't that true? Isn't that really what's going on? Yes or no, and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the instruction I was given by the department for victims and war crimes, I believe you are not entitled to offend me because you are trying to tie up my own person with something that I have nothing to do with. You call me a liar, and you are implying that I manipulated with human lives in order to justify crimes, and my answer to your question is a categorical no because that's merely your fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honour -- excuse me, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever is a liar is also a thief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're going to need to redact, and I think while we're redacting we should just go ahead and redact from page 12, line 15, all the way until page 15, line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that was an unnecessary intervention and an unhelpful one by Defence counsel for reasons which I think should be obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That we are in public session?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, that we have a witness in front of us and he just made a statement about another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have a -- one or two more brief topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified yesterday, sir, that civilians were killed in the attack on Saborsko, but let's be a little more precise and clear about that. You actually learned that civilians had been murdered in Saborsko, correct, that they had been deliberately killed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're forcing me to speculate once again. I said I knew this from the records after the sanitisation of the terrain. The records showed that there were women who were dead. When it said MUP members, that would imply enemy soldiers, but the reports actually mentioned women and men. So I learned this from the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in Plaski immediately following these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you learn either from records or from hearing or from any other source or knowledge that on the day of the attack on Saborsko on 12th of November, 1991, a 71-year-old woman by the name of Kata Matovina was killed by gunshot, Mato Matovina a 96-year-old man was killed by gunshot, Jure Vukovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. My learned friend can only say that these people died. Whether they were murdered, that's something that even the expert brought by the OTP could not say. He corrected himself and said that these people were killed in the firing, perhaps in the crossfire. To kill or murder is a very specific action. People were killed. There is no doubt there were corpses. But the -- my learned friend should say not that these people were murdered but that they died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'm not quite sure what it is you're objecting to on the question that was raised by Mr. Whiting. Mr. Whiting, when you, just before you stood up said, did you learn either from the records or from hearing or from any other source or knowledge that on the day of that attack on Saborsko on 12 November, 1991, a 71-year-old woman by the name of Kata Matovina was killed, not murdered, by gunshot. Mato Matovina, a 96-year-old man was killed by gunshot. Now you're talking about crossfire. Crossfire is still gunshot and killing results. So killing by gunshot. I don't know what the basis of your objection then is, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, Mr. Whiting talked about murder earlier. You didn't stand up. Now when you stand up, it's not using the word murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the interpreter has just corrected himself, but the interpretation I received and that the witness received was that the word "murdered" was used. The interpreter has now corrected himself and clarified the situation. It is as Your Honour said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I understand why you stood up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, nonetheless, I would object to objections that start feeding answers to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to go back to this topic. Did you learn, sir, that among the civilians killed that day was Kata Matovina, a 70-year-old woman who was killed by gunshot; Mato Matovina, a 96-year-old man killed by gunshot; Jure Vukovic, a 62-year-old man killed by gunshot. Did you learn about those people and how they were killed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know nothing about the circumstances of their killing. I only know of a certain number which I learned from the report on the sanitisation of the terrain. I didn't know those people while they were alive, and I cannot say anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you learn that some 14 civilians were buried in a pit near where the church was located, the big church in Saborsko? Was that part of the sanitisation?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When passing through Saborsko, when you go from the direction of Licka Jasenica, I often saw this row of wooden crosses. I didn't know exactly how many bodies were buried there. It was on the other side of the road than the church. The church is on the right-hand side, and this was about a hundred metres before you reach the church and on the other side of the road in a little depression, a kind of small valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, speaking of the church, sir, the big church in Saborsko was damaged during the attack on the 12th of November, 1991, but it was still standing, and it was mined and blown up some two to four weeks after the 12th of November, 1991. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I know nothing about this. I wasn't in Plasko at the time. I was in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were in Serbia two to four weeks after the 12th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I passed through Saborsko along that asphalt road in the direction of Korenica and Knin the church wasn't there. I don't know the time of its destruction or the manner of its destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was that? When did you see that it was no longer there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, Mr. Prosecutor, believe me. After the events in Saborsko, events happened very quickly. There was an attack on Slunj, a counter-attack. The brigade was established. There was an assembly in Knin, and then I went to Belgrade. So I didn't actually pass through Saborsko again until December.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So it was sometime in December of 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably. I can't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Fine. Now, to your knowledge, nobody among the forces, the armed forces that attacked Saborsko, was ever disciplined, investigated, or prosecuted for the crimes that occurred in Saborsko by the 12th of November -- on the 12th of November, 1991, by the authorities of the SAO Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't part of the judicial system.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, if you don't know -- sir, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So you have no knowledge of that. You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, finally -- the final topic I want to ask you about is something you said yesterday. It's at page 92 of the transcript, and you said, "Saborsko was turned into a stronghold when people from elsewhere were brought. You were able to see yourselves that Muslims were brought there, non-Catholics were brought to a Catholic area to have people under their command there." Now, you're talking about before November 12, 1991, here; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very specific. I said I was surprised when I saw that one of the three men who had been taken prisoners was a Muslim. He had been taken prisoner in the same group as Vlado Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was in September of 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you went on to say, this is still on page 92, "Nothing is sacred to those people. They sacrificed them deliberately because they knew that they would draw a response from the JNA. They needed human victims in order to attract the pity of Europe." So today as you sit there -- sit here in this courtroom, you actually believe, don't you, sir, that the Croats deliberately caused the murders of civilians in Saborsko in order to get the pity of Europe? That's what you believe, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that to the first group of European Community monitors who came to Plaski, and I compared this to people misusing their children and sending them begging in cities of western Europe. That's a comparison I used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you still believe that as you sit here today, don't you, sir? You haven't changed your view on that at all. You still believe it today; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should view these events in the context of the events of the time. You should see who was in power in Croatia at the time and who was making decisions in Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you just answer my question, please? You still believe that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm firmly convinced of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I put a few questions to the witness, I wish to draw attention to the fact that my learned friend has used up two and a half more time than the time used for the direct examination. In principle, the Defence has no objection to my learned friend doing his job, and we believe he needs to take as much time as he needs to arrive at important information, information important to him. The reason I'm saying this is that the Chamber should keep in mind that estimates are one thing, and without anybody being at fault, the time that actually has to be taken can be longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. The Chamber has to respond what you're saying, sir. I just want to say to you the Chamber is -- has noted the time taken by the Prosecution in cross-examination. The Chamber has noted the time taken by the Defence in leading this witness, and the Chamber has noted that the Prosecution also did indicate at the beginning of its cross-examination that there are issues that were raised by the Defence in the leading which had not been mentioned in the summary that was given to the Prosecution and that the Chamber does intend dealing with this question at the end of this witness's testimony and regrets that you raised this issue while the witness is here. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember, sir, that my learned friend asked you about the date when the victims at Glibodol Kriz were discovered. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you pointed to the log of Tactical Group 2, which says that between the 7th and 8th of November, 1991, it was discovered that three men were killed and their names are listed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I would ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What are you talking about? This log saying that the discovery was made between the 7th and the 8th? I don't remember that. The translation I got is do you remember that you pointed to that log of Tactical Group 2 which says that between the 7th and the 8th of November it was discovered that three men were killed. If this is really what we saw in this log.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was simply trying to introduce the topic and get the witness to know what we are talking about. I may have interpreted something in a way which is not the best way, but I am simply leading up to a question I want to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. Excuse me. Could we look at Exhibit 108. It's the operation log of Tactical Group 2. Page 3 in B/C/S, 7799 in the upper right-hand corner. And it's ordinal number 13, entry 13, that is, in the logbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the date next to entry 13? It says Glibodolski Kriz between the 7th and 8th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a page showing entries, 1, 2, 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please turn to page 3, 7799. Yes. Yes. Thank you. This is it. Entry 13 in the first column, it says Glibodolski Kriz between the 7th and 8th of November, 1991. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will read out the text to you. "Between the 7th and 8th of November, 1991, in the area of Glibodolski Kriz, three members of TO Plaski were killed as follows: Last name Susnjar, son of Vaso Stevo; and Susnjar, son of Djuro Milan; and Petrovic, son of Milan Bogdan." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And then in column 4 there's a signature. It's not very clear but can one say this is a signature?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the fifth column, it says "TO Plaski." This fifth column on the front page is entitled "Note." Do you see that it says "TO Plaski"?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Do you know how it was possible to establish that the three men bearing these names were killed? How could it have come to light that they were killed? They might have been missing or whatever. So what is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is that you can say someone has been killed when you find his body and establish that he is really dead and when the body is identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a part of Latas's report where it says that underneath the carcasses of two horses a human leg was discovered. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Prosecutor also showed you a part of the report which says, "We interrupted digging because night fell, and we continued on the following day"?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. That's also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this, in your opinion, confirm what you have just said, that the victims could have been identified only after they were dug up?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the leading nature of these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave I will withdraw my question and will not follow up on this in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me give you advice for what it is worth, Mr. Milovancevic, because I think the Chamber has talked about this to you a lot of times during this trial. You know, you weaken the weight of your own witness's testimony if you keep leading, and it doesn't help you to say, "Okay. I'm going to lead, and when I get caught I'm going to say I withdraw. Sorry, sorry." You have weakened your testimony already by that time. The weight to be attached to that -- this is counsel testifying, not the witness testifying. So I would like to urge you to please refrain from leading and just try to ask questions and not give answers. Let's get the answers from the witness. You -- this is your witness. The only person who can lead is the cross-examiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in principle I fully agree, but in this particular case I did not think I was putting a leading question because of the witness's previous answer. I wanted to bring things -- to carry this through all the way to the end, but as my learned friend raised an objection, I desisted. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, do you remember that you asked to be shown the front page of this report?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please have a look at page 1 of this log. 7797 in the upper right-hand corner. Yes. Let's look at columns 2 and 3, not column 1. So could we scroll down a bit. In column -- or, rather, in row 2, in entry 2, it says: "Slunj barracks, 4th November, 1991, 2200 hours." And next to it says: "At around 2200 hours, the forces of the MUP and ZNG illuminated the barracks in Slunj, and after that they opened fire from artillery weapons." Do you see this before you? This was on the 4th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In entry 3 where it says Slunj, and the date is the 5th of November, 1991, it says: "Around 1800 hours, from the area of Glibodolski Kriz, forces of the ZNG and MUP began firing on Licka Jasenica on the fuel depot in Licka Jasenica. The firing lasted until 2200 hours. Enemy forces fired from the areas of Alan and Veliki Sivnik. The fire was responded to by artillery fire with 26 shells."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was talking about. Let me remind you that Alan and Veliki Sivnik are elevations in the area of Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In entry 4 on this same page, again it says Slunj. The date is the 7th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we scroll down, because I don't see entry 4 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "Firing on the barracks, Licka Jasenica and forces of TO Plaski. Fire was opened from MB," and I believe this means mortar, "and a Browning by ZNG forces from the direction of Saborsko, Bozin Vhr and other directions."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and another elevation is mentioned but it's illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next page, 7798 in B/C/S. It's entry 5. It says: "5, Licka Jasenica, 7th of November, 1991." I won't read out the whole text because it's quite long, but in this first column there are many indications of the time, 1600 hours, 1630, 1645, 1700 hours, 2000 hours. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, all the way down to entry 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that next to entry 5 it says: "Licka Jasenica 7th of November, 1991." And it says: "Suffering strong firing from Saborsko and Glibodol on the barracks." And then in entry 6 it says: "Extremely strong attack on the barracks in Licka Jasenica by the ZNG."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And next to where it says 2000 hours in entry 8 it says: "One soldier killed. Barracks defended." Is this what you were talking about when answering to questions put both by the Defence and my learned friend? You were explaining that for three days you participated in fighting around the barracks in Licka Jasenica?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it says clearly that the TO positions are near to the barracks. That's in entry 8. So the operation of defending the barracks was finished on the 8th at 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it's a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, you looked at the contents of the operational log of the Tactical Group 2, the entry concerning the length of the attack on Licka Jasenica. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did that incident at Glibodolski Kriz take place as a result of which there were three human corpses and horse carcasses?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony I said that this took place in the period during which the attack lasted. I don't know when it took place, but it was uncovered on the 7th or 8th. I said I could not recall the date precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the Prosecutor asking you about the strength of Tactical Group 2?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let us please turn to one Prosecution document. According to my notes, this is 65 ter, document 1247. That is the only marking I have, unfortunately. You have before you this specific document. To gain time, I will read what is contained in the upper-left corner. "5th military district command, strictly confidential, 23rd October, 1991." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the text below the setting up of Tactical Group 2 order?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the text immediately below the title we have just read out? The text reads as follows: "Pursuant to the directive of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence for the use of forces," and I will now skip the numbers, "dated 20 September 1991, and based on the need that has arisen and with a view to making the command and control system more efficient, I hereby order." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, on the matter of the strength of Tactical Group 2, I will read out item 1 of the order, which says: "Setting up TG-2 with the following composition," and now we have several entries there. I will read them out, not the abbreviations that are stated here but the full text, and you will tell me whether this corresponds in fact to the text here. Therefore, "I order under 1 to set up TG-2 of the following make-up." First entry: "Armoured battalion of the 4th armoured brigade." Next entry: "Mixed artillery battalion of 560th mixed artillery brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just -- since this is re-examination, I'm just wondering why it wouldn't be better just to let the witness read the abbreviations and says what he knows about them rather than counsel giving his version of what the abbreviations mean and leading the witness that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree. Perhaps the witness should start from the beginning. If that will make the matters more clear, then I agree, but I wanted to save us time. Please start reading from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Set up TG-2 of the following make-up: Armoured battalion from the 4th armoured brigade. Next entry: Mixed artillery battalion, abbreviation MAD, from the 506th mixed artillery brigade. Third entry: Light anti-aircraft artillery battalion (mixed of 306th light artillery regiment of the anti-aircraft defence). 185th Slunj training grounds signals platoon from 367th Signals Regiment. Security company from the mixed" -- I'm not sure about the -- "65th ZATP Reconnaissance Platoon. Platoon from 113th Engineers Brigade and then the automobile squad from" -- I'm not sure about 243rd. I believe the automobile unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The text you just read out, based on your knowledge and knowledge of the terrain is consistent with what TG-2 consisted of?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And these forces were mostly stationed at the Slunj training grounds, all the forces mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since it is possible for the term "divisione" in B/C/S to cause confusion, because it may be confused with "divisione." Can you please explain for us what this is? The second entry says "MAD, mixed artillery divisione." What is that unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1985, 1986, I served the army in Zadar in the artillery branch, and I know that the mixed artillery divisione or artillery battalion consists of several batteries. The battery corresponds to a company in the infantry forces, and the battery is used for artillery units. The MAD abbreviation is normally used in reference to artillery pieces such as howitzers and in reference to anti-armour combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In item 3 of this order it is stated: "The task of the command of TG-2 is to coordinate the activities of the units of the JNA in the Slunj training grounds." Could we please scroll down a bit to see item 3 in its entirety. Thank you. "Therefore, the task of TG-2 is to unify, coordinate the activities of the JNA units in the Slunj training grounds and the units of the TO [indiscernible] in Plaski, in the area of responsibility." Were there -- were their activities, in fact coordinated?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of all these locations mentioned here and I went to all these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need this document any more. Could we please look at the following document, Exhibit 52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I wonder if I could hear a bit more about a battery and what the function of the battery is, how it operates. I'm interested to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, you've heard Her Honour Judge Nosworthy. Can you tell us what is a battery in the framework of artillery?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The battery is the basic unit consisting of several platoons. Each platoon must have at least two artillery pieces which can be either a cannon or a 120-millimetre mortar or a howitzer. The battery, therefore, consists of four to six artillery pieces, either mortars, howitzers, or cannons. There was at least at the time I served the obligatory military service, but I don't think much had changed in these five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do you wish us to expound on this issue of batteries or does this suffice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It will suffice for the time being. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I would just like to add that we discuss now Exhibit 50, court Exhibit 50, and now you are changing the subject, aren't you? Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, that's correct. Can we please now turn to Exhibit 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, you recall the Prosecutor showing you the order issued by the 13th command -- 13th Corps Command addressed to the command of Tactical Group 2. This document was also shown to you in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor read out item 1 of the order, which we can see now on our screens, and it reads: "Order for attack." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Item 1 reads: "The forces of MUP and ZNG of Croatia have for some time now been fortifying themselves in the sectors of Borik Hill, the villages of Saborsko, Funtana, Panjici and Kuselj." I will skip one part just to remind you of the text. "Toward the end of the paragraph the Prosecutor quoted that the enemy was not organising classical defence but was getting entrenched and using the pillbox system of gun machine emplacements and buildings (basements)." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Within item 1 the locations where enemy forces are stationed are mentioned, and one entry reads as follows: "In the area of the village of Borik, there are six gun machine emplacements, and at the edge of the village or to the south of the village around 50 Ustashas are located." It goes on to say that: "To the south of the village of Tuk there is a light machine-gun emplacement and in the area to the north-west -- or to the area to the south of the village there were two gun machine emplacements. Then to the north-west of Alan, an unknown number are stationed and in the nearby grove there are 200 Ustashas and the air forces fired upon them. In the village of Saborsko, the strength of the enemy is estimated at 150 Ustashas and the same number of them is estimated to be stationed in the village of Funtana. In the slopes of Mali Sevnic, 82-millimetre mortars in unknown numbers and to the west there are light machine-gun and machine-gun emplacements. And to the south of that area on the dirt road there, there are also gun machine emplacements. And then in the village of Kusan, again, the presence of the enemy was detected but the numbers are unknown." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of the document, right below the text we've just been reading, below item 3 or, rather, midway through item 3, the following words are contained that's 7774, "I hereby order." That's the very top of page 7774. That's page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. Suddenly my English version has disappeared from my screen and the B/C/S version has jumped up on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have page 2 in B/C/S. I'd like to know whether the difficulty you had with your version has been solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us what paragraph are you looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What paragraph are you reading at page 2. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for your benefit, this order has detailed specific orders under items 1, 2, 3. We are looking at -- at item 3, the third paragraph of item 3, which starts with the following words: "I hereby -- I have decided". And it goes on to say: "From --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, I will put only some portions of the text to you, and I will be skipping others to show you what the aim of the order is. "I have decided to carry out an order in the villages of Kusan and Funtana and Licka Jasenica and Saborsko with the following objective: Along the mentioned axis, crush and destroy the enemy formations in the area of Saborsko, prevent them from pulling out to the north and thus definitely crush their resistance in the area." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The next item is item 5. Item 5 again contains a part of the order relating to the 5th Partisan Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You know, Your Honour, I don't want to kind of delay things even more than they are, but I'm just not sure I see the point in reading out this document point by point which is already in evidence. There have been no real questions about -- it's just is this in the order, is this in the order and that was the same with one of the previous exhibits and I just don't see the point of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm just sort of trying to exercise my patience to wait for a question. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it won't take long, and I would really ask for you to be patient. I think it's very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, item 5 of the order reads that -- or, rather, let's look at line 3 of item 5. "We'll attack along the axis of the villages of Kusan and Funtana with the following task: The forceful engagement of the tanks and infantry should crush the enemy present along the mentioned axis." Do you see that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In item 7 of the order entitled "Fire support," can we please scroll down to see item 7, "Fire support." Under (A), air support. "As part of fire preparations, air force will launch an attack to neutralise the targets in the areas of villages of Borik, Alan, Saborsko, and the village of Funtana." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under (B) it says artillery support. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Below the heading "Tasks," under artillery support --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which is on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's on page 3 in B/C/S, and then we will come to the end of the part of the document that is of interest to us. Within item 7 we're turning to page 3 in B/C/S, which is page 7775, and there the tasks of artillery support are listed. "The rocket launcher, 128-millimetre, will be active with the following tasks," and then you have the tasks. "Neutralise, and there are abbreviations ZS and VS of the enemy in the sectors of the villages of Borik, Tuk, Brdine, Alan and the village of Saborsko." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this "neutralise Z/S V/S of the enemy," what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Z/S means manpower and V/S means weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that the task of TG-2 is to neutralise the manpower and the weaponry of the enemy in the areas mentioned therein?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Finally, does this order or any other order that has been presented to you here state as a target objective or axis of engagement to -- or, rather, does it state as a target objective or axis of engagement Glibodolski Kriz?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've finished with this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask the witness about this document one general question. Who is the author of this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the beginning we said it said command of the 13th corps, forward command post, village of Mukinje, Plitvice. I looked at the signature. This colonel later became General Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And how does this document look like to you? This is a carbon copy, it seems, with some added words in the beginning. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the beginning of the document now. I can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... page 1 of the B/C/S original. Of the B/C/S original, yes. I'm addressing the question of authenticity of this document. This seems to be a carbon copy, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I see, it does look like a copy, because in the corner you can see where it was stapled together, and in the upper right-hand corner underneath where it says "Military secret, strictly confidential," it says: "Hand over directly to the forward command post 13th Mukinje at 0730 hours, 9th of November, 1991." This means that whoever wrote this was writing on the 7th and the order was that it should be handed over directly at the forward command post two days later on the 9th of November. And section 1 toward -- 1:50000, referring to Bihac 1, Karlovac 3, Ogulin 4 and Gospic 2 is typed differently. These are military maps where you can see the layout of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And have you seen this document before, or only here in the trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not addressed to company commanders. I did not receive any written orders. The battalion commander only told me the axes and the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Would you regard this document authentic, a real order of that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, especially in view of the fact that certain abbreviations are skipped over which only the JNA used. I mean when counsel was reading allowed, he skipped over some things such as TT, meaning trig point, and other abbreviations which I remember were used by the JNA. This is the form, the pattern in which orders were issued in that army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the fact that there is a signature but no stamp at the end as we saw that doesn't cause any special doubts about authenticity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe that military units at that level had stamps. It was the military post that used to have those stamps. It would say VP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was all about this document. Please, my -- oh, just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this document which we have just shown you and discussed, can you tell us one thing, please. In your opinion, the events at Glibodolski Kriz, that is the cruel murder of three territorials, was that the reason why this order was issued by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two events are not connected at all. Evidently the commander of the 13th Corps and the Operative Group and the commander of Tactical Group 2 did not know that this had occurred when they wrote these orders. There's a difference in time, and it's clear from these documents. I think these are two entirely separate events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Medakovic, when you mentioned the action in Saborsko and linked it to the events at Glibodolski Kriz, why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm wondering if it could be clarified when he's talking about. Is he talking about in his letter of the 13th of November, or is he talking about in his testimony here in court on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, both. It is both. The letter cannot be separated from his testimony, especially in view of these numerous questions. So in view of his entire testimony and all his explanations, I'm asking why he mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I explained yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has to rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, there's nothing to rule on because it's just a request that you explain what you are linking it to and you have explained. What I wanted to find out from Mr. Whiting and Judge Hoepfel was whether they're satisfied with your answer. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This would make it a double question, actually. Maybe you can ask it for the letter and then maybe for some statement here. These are two different actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you spoke in detail about that letter. Can you add anything to the explanation you gave, or do you wish to change something, or do you still abide by it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I abide by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's sufficient. When you mentioned Glibodolski Kriz in your testimony here, and the action in Saborsko, what kind of connection did you make between the two?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of the action took place after the events at Glibodolski Kriz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that my learned friend asked you how it came about that Plaski was blocked, and you said that you went towards Gracac or Vrhovine at least twice a month. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you replied that on two occasions or, rather, at least twice a month you took a forest trail to Vrhovine and that your life was always in danger?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I first said always, then often, and then the Prosecutor made an inappropriate remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's remark to what you said about your life being threatened. Let me ask you this: Did others use those forest trails in order to reach certain destinations? I'm referring to civilians, to other people from Plaski and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that that forest trail was used only in cases of extreme necessity, and those three poor people who ended up the way they did at Glibodolski Kriz used it. I had to use it because I had to maintain links with the rest of the Krajina. As I was the top man in this conference of municipalities of ours, later our municipality, and we had no telephone connections, we had to rely on personal visits and couriers. We tried to secure the road so that children could go to school, to Rudo Polje. We secured the route and took the children to Rudo Polje no foot risking terrible things along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What terrible things?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a forest trail which one could reach from various directions, Lipice, and others.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch them all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these four directions converge, and someone could approach without being seen by you. It was a place where ambushes could easily be set, and many incidents occurred there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say it was a place where ambushes could easily be set, who did that? Who -- who laid ambushes?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the MUP and the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what were the results of these incidents? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the results were that from the area of Dabar, that's a village which you arrive at when you go from Licka Jasenica through the Glibodolski crossing and go straight ahead you come to the village of Dabar which is a mixed village but there were more Serbs there by far, and they had a kind of Territorial Defence company there, and on that road they suffered terrible losses. In the course of only one day, seven people were taken away. Some of them, unfortunately, were minors. They were tortured and killed. And the only exchange carried out when urns containing ashes were returned to the Serb side this happened in Dabar in November 1991. No one has mentioned this here yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Sorry. Why do you say people were either killed or murdered, but why do you mention these urns? What do they have to do with it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, let me just ask a question. The witness has just said now that nobody has mentioned this in this court. This is completely new evidence, if I am not mistaken. Of what relevance is it to the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend made a sarcastic remark when Witness Medakovic said that every time he used a forest trail his life was in danger. He didn't put a question. He just said, really? The witness noticed this. The Prosecutor insists that other roads would have been used, either this long training ground or through the mountains or through the woods. It seems that the Prosecutor thinks this is all the same and it's very relevant to establish whether it was possible to pass through and how. So this is not a new area. It's a response to questions put by the Prosecutor. I will not go further into the events in Dabar. I did not know about this piece of information that the witness is now presenting. That's why I asked. I'm checking to see whether what the witness says is logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As you mentioned urns, why urns? Did you talk about urns of people from Dabar?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain what happened. After the Sarajevo truce was signed in late 1991 or early 1992, there was an all for all exchange of prisoners of war and bodies of those killed on both sides. I think that the JNA commission for negotiations was headed by Colonel Svetozar Marjanovic, and if I'm not mistaken, it's the same colonel who signed another agreement. This colonel received these urns from the Croatian sides, and seven names were provided. The rumours were that these bodies were so disfigured that they didn't want them to be seen. In Croatia there are not so many crematoriums, so the question is who cremated the bodies and what they looked like before the cremation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit 23. It's an atlas we often use. The page is page 19. The -- my learned friend gave a number for the page, but I don't have it now. I believe it is page 19. It should be easy to find. 19

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: [B/C/S on English channel]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Maybe we can enlarge the region between Ogulin and Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's precisely what I was about to ask. On page 19, the area between Ogulin and Plitvice, could we zoom in on that, please. That's the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: In the middle of the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the left-hand side. We're looking for the right-hand side. And could we scroll down a bit. We see Ogulin now. Can we -- oh, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, do you see the map?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher hand Mr. Medakovic a marker which he could use to mark the places he mentioned on this atlas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can we zoom in it would be a very good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could zoom in it would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The very upper end and Otocac and Plitvice in the lower end. And Plaski would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not identifying Plitvice. I saw a reference to Plaski right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Right lower corner, the lakes, you'll see that. But zoom in a little more. Just click on Plaski so it's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Below Poljanak, Your Honours, yes. Plitvice are underneath Poljanak in the right-hand corner, the lower right-hand corner. This is enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... between Plaski, Saborsko, Glibodol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please focus on Ogulin again on the map. It's in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please, would you first circle Plaski on this map, Mr. Medakovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you now circle Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your evidence, you mentioned Josipdol and Skradnik. Could you please circle those always well.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned Slunj. Please circle it.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Dabar, Stajnica and Lipice. Circle them as well.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned Vrhovine. I not sure whether we can see it on the map. Perhaps we should scroll up a bit. Or, rather, scroll down so we can see the top of the map. Let us see the top of the map. I'm not sure if we actually have to scroll down or up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't know but I think you lose the marks if you scroll down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that's enough. I thank my learned friend. I don't think we should deal with this. We will deal with the other place later on. I would like to keep this as a document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I'm hearing the English interpretation now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we help the witness, please, to make sure he hears the correct interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, can you tell us, at the time of the events you testified about, in 1990, 1991, up until the November attack on Saborsko, in which of these locations were MUP and ZNG forces stationed?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Skradnik, Josipdol, Stajnica, Modrusa which is one place along the road from Josipdol to Kapela.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please circle Modrus.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes this is the road all the way to Stajnica. Lipice. The village of Dabar was under our control and Drenov Klanac and Brlog at the very bottom of the map was already in the hands of MUP and ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And Saborsko was under whose control?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the control of the MUP and ZNG as were all the locations along the main road to Saborsko across Poljanak, Krakovice and then to Slunj. Rakovice, Poljanak, Saborsko were all places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please circle them.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that in addition to Plaski in the middle and Dabar for which you said was a mixed village all the other locations were under the control of MUP and ZNG forces at the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was also Kamenica, Stradnicka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please circle it.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gornje Premise was under Serb control. Gornji Blagaj under the Croatian control, and all the places from Slunj to Velubno. Velunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please draw a line from Slunj to Velunj. I wish to tender this document into evidence as a Defence exhibit, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Save it you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Save the page you mean with the markings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
