utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I wanted this page containing these markings to be admitted into evidence. Judge Nosworthy, I'm sorry, we interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No, no. It's quite all right. I was just wondering if there was some way of distinguishing where the MUP and ZNG forces were stationed and where the Serb forces were stationed. It's all ringed in red now. I wondered if to add greater clarity there was some way of making the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for this suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please place a cross on the locations where MUP and ZNG forces were stationed, and this is how we shall interpret them later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This remark, we discussed more or less only such places and we didn't go into the details where Serb forces were stationed. It wasn't the only places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought the witness had mentioned where Serb forces were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Was that the only two places you mentioned, Plaski and -- what was the other one, Licka Jasenica, where Serb forces were stationed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Halfway between Plaski and Josipdol was where the separation line was. These are inhabited areas, and the front line was closer to Plaski on all the sides. Licka Jasenica is an inhabited place as is Jezero, and that's where the Serb forces were stationed, namely TO. Plaski is the largest inhabited place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do think that this has now gone way beyond anything I asked on cross-examination. It's new evidence which could have been elicited in the direct examination. You know, for example, he's now talking about Poljanak which consistently in cross-examination he said he knew nothing about and now he's making representations about what happened there. So I'm just a little bit -- I think this really has gone beyond anything that I asked about on the cross-examination. This is all new, new evidence that is coming in. Also, we don't know what dates we are talking about. This is sort of vague time periods. I think this has gone beyond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I find it hard to agree with my learned friend. My learned friend has in the course of cross-examination asked about the actions of MUP and ZNG forces from Ogulin and Saborsko toward Glibodolski Kriz. He asked about the conflict on the 22nd of July near Ostarije and Josipdol. He spoke of the front line. He mentioned all these places, and he claimed -- and this particular map has to do with the part of the cross-examination where the Prosecutor stated that the Serbs from Plaski could move freely and that it was no hindrance to them the fact that the road was blocked. I wanted the Bench to have an idea of where these locations are and where the forces were stationed so that you can interpret what the witness is testifying about and to see the points made both by the Prosecution and Defence. Therefore, I can't see how this document can be superfluous, especially with regard to the fact that the Prosecutor used maps in his examination of this very area and of -- involving these very locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The only problem about what I see about what's happening now, Mr. Milovancevic, is that you're giving details of positions of these -- whatever you call these MUPs and what have you, which you should have done in your examination-in-chief. You're now behaving like a cross-examiner instead of a re-examiner, and that is the only problem I have with this. Surely it was within your power to lead this evidence in its entirety in the beginning to show why the MUP of the -- of the JNA or the JNA itself took the particular routes that it took because other routes were blocked by the MUP of the ZNG. You're coming up with this -- this necessitates a further cross-examination of this witness on these issues. This is the problem. Because it is now new evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm telling you, unless you're saying I'm wrong. And I don't deny that I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me, please, to be of assistance. Since His Honour Judge Moloto addressed me, I ask my learned friend to allow me to go first. In direct examination, the witness mentioned each and every one of these locations as the locations where the Croatian forces were stationed at. The only thing we didn't do was mark these places on the map. Since in the course of cross-examination the Prosecutor insisted on matters that were the opposite of what the witness stated, I wanted to have them down on the map. There is not a single new piece of evidence of fact here except that we are able to see these locations now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... mentioned in evidence in chief then there's no need to repeat them. You're just rehashing the evidence in chief again and it is unfortunately taking a lot of the precious time that we need to finalise the case. You don't need to rehash. Whether you did mark them or didn't mark them, they are in evidence. Exhibit 23 is an exhibit. When the judgement has been drafted, we will look at them and we will circle them. We'll say, what date did they mention these places? Where are they on the map? We'll find them. Circling them if you have mentioned them doesn't take your case any further. But anyway, before I ask Judge Hoepfel to say something, Mr. Whiting, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to drag this out, but I would respond to two things. One, I never suggested that the Serbs could move freely. I only suggested that this witness was able to travel outside of Plaski two times a month and that's all I put to him. So this elaborate long re-examination based on that point to show, you know, where the forces were in the whole region is not justified by that. The second point is that it's not true that all of these locations were mentioned. That's not true. In fact, the contrary. It is the contrary. And I would object to this being made an exhibit and I think we should move on in the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is exactly what I wanted to say, that I don't remember all these places having been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't remember myself, but I was saying -- assuming that short memory and particularly because I'm dealing with names that I don't know. It is in this that all of these names were mentioned in evidence in-chief. Mr. Milovancevic, as a result, there is an objection to that admission of this page. Do you have a response to the objection? We have moved away from what you were saying now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Also to the examination in cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have come to the very end of my re-examination. This was my last question. I just wanted to state this clearly. That's one point. The other point is that the witness, at the outset of his direct examination explained the setting up of the association of local communes involving Plaski and all the other places and he clearly listed the places where the Croats were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you. Not Croats being the majority, where the MUPs were existing. Can you refer us to the text on the transcript in the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... standing there and trying to explain. Just refer us to where the witness mentioned all these names in the examination, because I've got to rule on the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find it now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You'd better find them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I can inquire -- Your Honour, I desist from this question. If this is causing confusion, well, then this is something I do not need. I cannot find it at this time. I withdraw this question, and I find what the witness says stated so far sufficient. Therefore, the map need not be admitted into evidence as a document. I believe my questions will suffice. My re-examination is complete, and I thank the witness for his patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. The objection is upheld and the -- that page will not be made an exhibit or be saved as -- in the form in which it was circled. Any questions, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: While we have this on the screen, I would like you to give us an idea about the distance between certain locations. First, how many kilometres it is between Plaski centre and Ogulin centre about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have to tell you approximately. It's exactly 26 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I'm assuming you would know that. And then Plaski to Licka Jasenica it's something like 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Between Licka Jasenica and Saborsko it's 6 or something.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly 6 to 7 depending on which part of Saborsko you're looking at. I don't have the map anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Saborsko is a street -- village and then of course there's different distances. Yes. That's about all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. I do have a couple of questions. Mr. Medakovic, is it? I wanted to ask you about the training at Gula beach. Who was it who trained you? Who gave you your training?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By coincidence, my instructor and commander was one and the same person, Stevo Plejo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure about the last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last name for the purposes of our interpreter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The witness who testified before me in this case, Stevo Plejo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What were the ages of the persons being trained with you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The eldest was around 40, and the rest were between 25 and 30 years of age, but most of them were young-ish people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Whilst you were receiving your training at Golubic, did you see the accused, Mr. Martic, there at any time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The training took place outside the area except for the training that took place on a concrete strip. We would go out into the forest. I had occasion to see only my immediate commander. The training would start with jogging, a 7 kilometre jog, and then we would have other training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please bear in mind the question I had asked you, which was whether or not you had seen the accused whilst you were training at Golubic. You're taking the point that your training did not take place there but it took place elsewhere. So maybe you could answer in respect of the two. Firstly, where it is that you physically had your training. Did you see the accused at any time and also did you see him at Golubic training ground?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my evidence here, I stated that I saw him before I went for my training. During the training I no longer saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. So the answer is a simple no.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Yes. You asked me where the training took place. As one left the compound, there was a small pine wood there and a lake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... took place. You actually gave that answer to me, but I really wanted to find out about Mr. Martic and whether you had seen him at any of those two locations, and I take it that in relation to the training ground, you are saying, no, you did not see him at Golubic, nor when you were doing your training. And I'm going to leave that area now unless your answer has been misunderstood by me. The next question for my own education, in military terms, what is an axis?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Axis, if it's been interpreted well, well, the axis means the direction of the attack. You have the starting point and then a line leading you to another place. So we will move along the axis, meaning the line connecting two places, the point of departure and the point of arrival.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It may be a gender thing, because my two male colleagues do not appear to be in difficulty there. I'm going to go on to another area now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I appreciate your clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge Hoepfel for reassuring me. I'm not at a disability by virtue of my gender. It has to do with the functions of the Special Purpose Unit, and I believe you gave your evidence and you said in part the function was to materialise the will of the people. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I must confess that I didn't quite understand what you meant, and I would like you to tell me what it means, to materialise the will of the people as one of the duties of the Special Purpose Unit.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The will of the people as expressed at the referendum on annexing to Krajina and on abandoning the Korenica municipality. This meant that the local communes of Vojnovac, Latine, Plaski, Plavca Draga, Jajan Goran, Licka Jasenica would operate as an area secured by the police forces loyal to the SUP of Krajina. This was the will of the majority of the people expressed at the referendum. We merely operationalised it, which meant that we had our own police force on our own territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So how would the will of the people be effected or materialised?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely by establishing full control over the material, preventing the arrival of the Croatian police, and that police force was not welcome at the time. If there is the Krajina police force, then the MUP of Croatia can no longer have any authority there. They're mutually exclusively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I crave your indulgence. One moment, please. Thank you very much, Mr. Medakovic. I'm finished. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Medakovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm also going to start off by asking you questions relating to your military -- your training at Golubic. When you gave your evidence in-chief, I remember you saying something to -- I'm not quoting you, but I'm just sort of giving you the subject that you talked about. When you talked about your training, you said you were jumping off wooden walls, and it was a simple military training. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember saying that we would descend wooden wall. We would be descending along ropes. And then I don't know if I mentioned that the first day we were instructed how to load and unload a rifle, which I found quite elementary. But we were divided into small groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You did mention that, yes. You did mention that you were taught on how to load and unload a rifle, and you did say you found it quite elementary because you had undergone military training. What I'm trying to suggest -- what I'm trying to find out from you is that having told us what you went through, you gave a general description of the training, and you said simple military training. Do you remember that? I'd like you to focus on that.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I spoke of the police training of the special police force. I don't think that I used the term "military," although the training is quite similar. I said that we had the training for marching group, about left, about right, and those sort of orders, when we were in a line. So that's the term I might have used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm telling you the term you used. You said "Simple military training." I might not be able to get you to that because these pages change every day and I'm not sufficiently computer literate when the pages have changed. It's better to ask you questions on the same day as you testified, then I can refer to the pages correctly. But this was quite early in your testimony, and I'm going to try and find the place.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how this -- oh, it's drill. It's drill. This is the training --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Don't talk too much. Let's find the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is page 8969, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't have that page. I still have page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The 9th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I must click on 9th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, in the English it says at page 8969: "We spent the longest time on establishment, movement, sweeping of terrain. Simple military training. Getting to know your weapons, how to handle them and so on." That's the answer from you as we've got it on the transcript. Okay? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says. I didn't say cleansing, I said sweeping of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't say cleansing either. I said sweeping. Just a minute. I'll tell you what I said. Yes, what we've got here is sweeping. But be that as it may, it's time now for the break. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00, and we'll carry on when you come back. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, before we went on the break, you were saying that you did not use the word "sweeping," you used the word "cleansing," and so that -- or the other way around, or whatever it is. So that we can move forward and not waste time, that's not where I'm focusing my attention at the moment, and I'm prepared to concede that we use the word you want used there. What I do want you to concentrate on, and please try to concentrate on what I'm saying, is the little sentence composed of three words "Simple military training." Remember that? Can you see it now on the screen? Well, you may not see it on the screen, but do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm certain I said "simple drill." I don't know how the word "drill" was interpreted. I did not use the term "military training," because I had done my military service and I know what military service implies. I had even been a squad leader in the JNA. We had simple drills.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Be that as it may, after your training, one of the things that you did with your group was to form the right flank of the attack on Saborsko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can't say after the training. It was six months after the training, Your Honours, and the unit no longer existed as such. I was not its commander at the time that I commanded the group that was in the right flank. I spoke about that at length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What unit did you command when you were commanding -- when you formed part of the right flank of the attack on Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit that was assigned to me numbered about 60 men. They comprised active-duty and reserve policemen, police who had formerly been part of that unit which I led to Knin, and volunteers from other parts of the Plaski Territorial Defence brigade. Altogether, the manpower was about 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Therefore, some of the people that you were with -- in training with in Knin were part of the 60 men that you commanded when you were -- when you formed the right flank of the attack on Saborsko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was part of the materialising of the will of the people, was it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not linking up the two. What I said was that on our return from our training, we materialised the will of the people, because apart from that police squad, we also did policework within the conference of local communes. So my response when I spoke about materialising the will of the people, this did not refer to Saborsko. There is a time distance of six months between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that you are not saying so, but I am -- please listen to my questions. I'm trying to find out -- you said that -- you explained that by materialising the will of the people was to ensure that the Croatian MUP doesn't come into your way and you fend them off, and I'm just asking you whether it would be fair to say that that -- being part of the right flank of the attack on Saborsko was part of the materialising of that will of the people. And you can just say yes, it was, or no, it was not. You don't have to give me a long explanation.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was part of the operation carried out by Tactical Group 2. I had clear orders as to what I was to do, very clear and precise, specific orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So your answer is really that you were not trained in military-work, in military functions when you were in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I'll leave that topic now. You mentioned that from Golubic you were supplied with uniforms and weapons. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was interpreted to me "from there." When we arrived there, we arrived in civilian clothes and unarmed. When we started our training, we were issued with personal weapons, boots, and a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I implore you once again to please listen to my questions and answer my questions. You know, if I want a full explanation from you, I'll ask for it. What I'm asking you is you were supplied from Golubic with uniforms and weapons. Is it correct or is it not correct? Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only for those who underwent training. Only the men who went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of course I'm talking about the men who were undergoing training. Just say yes or say no, sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Can you describe the uniforms that you were supplied with in detail, please? Now I want an explanation from you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember well, Your Honours. We received two-piece camouflage uniforms. On the sleeve there was the patch shown to me here, semi-circular with the words milicija and Krajina with the Serbian tricolour. We received ankle high boots and on the uniform there was a piece of canvas I found on the uniform with a handwritten message saying may God protect your brother. These were messages from the women who sewed the uniforms. And I kept that piece of canvas with me for a long time. So these were two-piece camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that all?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't have caps those first days, but later on some people got berets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any patch on the berets?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the Serbian tricolour, but I'm not certain. I received one which was a camouflage beret with no markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned also in your evidence that you made no ethnic distinctions in the beginning that in fact you had friends among Croats and you all grew up together. Remember that? I'm probably embellishing a little bit, but you made no ethnic distinctions in the beginning. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We didn't grow up together. I grew up in an exclusively Serb community, but we went to school together. When I went to school in Plaski and Ogulin there were some Croats in our class. In fact, in Ogulin they were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if you make no ethnic -- if there were no ethnic distinctions being made -- before I say that, do you also remember saying that you had a checkpoint along the ethnic boundary of Vojnovac?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can't say that there were many of them. There was only one at the ramp, at the barricades in Vojnovac. The railway, the railway barrier that is. There was a crossing between the railway track and the asphalt road, and there was a barrier there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please listen to my questions and please answer my questions. Don't formulate questions for yourself and then go ahead and answer them. I didn't suggest that there were many. I've said: You said in your evidence that there was a checkpoint along the ethnic boundary of Vojnovac. That's one. That's not many. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, don't waste time. Now, surely if there is this kind of ethnic geographic distinction, then ethnic distinctions were being made.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ethnic distinction ran along the border of the local commune, which through a referendum --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I must interrupt you. Ethnic distinctions were being made. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borders of territories were drawn up where there was a majority of Croats and a majority of Serbs. We controlled the territory where there was a large Serb majority. On the other side were the Croats and their police. That was the ethnic distinction and the ethnic border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So -- and this was done in various areas. Each area had -- was known to be either a majority Croat or a majority Serb. Isn't it so? If not hundred per cent Croat or hundred per cent Serb.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were a compact community surrounded on all sides by a Croat majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. Croat geographic majorities. So there were geographic ethnic distinctions being made. They were not just made socially. They were not just made mentally, recorded mentally. They were actually there geographically, physically on the ground, these distinctions.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb people had a referendum where they declared that they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. I'm sorry. I'm not asking you about a referendum. I'm talking to you about distinctions that were being made on the ground geographically even before the referendum. Villages and towns composed of predominantly either Croats or predominantly Serbs. There were geographic distinctions, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't understand the term "geographic differences." That's how it was interpreted to me. Distinctions, geographic distinctions. Geography is unified. You can't divide hills and valleys. It's not clear to me. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. I'll try to explain myself. The town, for instance, or the village of Saborsko would have been a village composed either entirely or predominantly of a particular ethnic group. Is it not so?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And some other village, let us say, for instance, Slunj or Poljanak, would be composed of predominantly some other ethnic group. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case Slunj and Poljanak were inhabited by the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. That is so. Now, that is what I mean by geographic distinction, is that if you look at the geography of Saborsko, it is entirely Croat or predominantly Croat. Some other little area within the same Krajina or within the same Croatia or within the same former Yugoslavia would still -- would be predominantly a particular ethnic group. Do you now understand what I mean by geographic ethnic distinctions? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I'm saying to you -- now that we understand what we mean by geographic ethnic distinction, I'm saying to you these geographic ethnic distinctions were there. They existed.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For hundreds of years, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Therefore, it is not absolutely correct to say that you made no ethnic distinctions. You knew in your sleep that a particular village was predominantly Croat or Serb.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't deny that. That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't say you denied that. All I said is that you said in evidence you made no ethnic distinctions. I'm saying, therefore, it wasn't correct to say such ethnic distinctions were not made.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to specific events and specific names, and if need be I can repeat, Your Honour. When looking for a job, if I was the boss, the one who made the decision, I didn't make any distinctions. If there was a Serb lawyer and a Croat lawyer applying for the same job, they had an equal chance of getting that job, and the criterion used was their expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's not what I was asking for. Now, Savo, I'm not sure whether I'll be able to pronounce the second name, Trbojevic, where was he trained?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I think he did his regular military service. He's some 15 years my senior, maybe more, maybe 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you said that he was a commander of a platoon during the attack, isn't it? Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And he was part of the army that attacked Saborsko. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And after the attack on Saborsko, you said he led the looting of Saborsko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not precisely the way I put it. I said that his duty was to remain there and secure the battlefield. So he let it happen. The commander of the company who was his superior told me that when we met up at the command post after the end of the action. He said to me a platoon commanded by Savo Trbojevic has been left there to secure the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll read to you page 14 of today's proceedings at line 20. Let me start at line 17 where the question is put to you. "The truth is, sir, he did not command any plan, and he did not have any responsibility, or he was not responsible for the looting and burning that occurred in Saborsko, was he?" Your answer was: "He was the one who led the looting exercise in Saborsko and in Glibodol. I know that even in front of his house there was a gun showdown because they were vying over war booty." Now, the transcript shows that you said he led the looting exercise in Saborsko. Are you --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, please. There are several misinterpretations here. First I said Saborsko and Glibodol. The event was in Glibodol. That operation was a little -- took place a little later than the operation in Saborsko. And I didn't say he was showing his weapons. What I said was that they argued over who would get a knitting machine, he and his workmates. I got this information from his best man. They were brandishing pistols, arguing over a knitting machine from Glibodol. I wanted to use this incident to illustrate the character of that man. He said something about me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, please understand that I don't know B/C/S. I know English. I can only read to you what is translated to me, and unfortunately we don't have the record in B/C/S. I'm saying to you and I'm reading to you what's written here. Your answer was: "He was the one who led the looting exercise in Saborsko and in Glibodol. I know that even in front of his house there was a gun showdown because they were vying over the war booty." That's what is said here. Now, do you agree with that or you don't agree with that? Just say yes or no. Don't give me a long explanation. Because now you're telling me about knitting machines, and I don't remember seeing anything about knitting machines on the transcript or even hearing anything about a knitting machine. Did you say what I've just told you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as for the second version you read to me, yes, it was interpreted differently than the first time. The first time it was interpreted that a gun was shown, a rifle, but this time it was interpreted correctly. There was a showdown because of an argument about the distribution of stolen property, and I told you where I heard this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. Just -- now, understand that my concentration and my focus is not on the showdown but it is on the leading of this looting. Do you accept that that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to lead is perhaps putting it too strongly, but I'm certain he participated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to interpret what is written here. I'm asking you if this is what you said. Just tell me if this is what you said or didn't say. The word "led," as I understand it, comes from your mouth if the interpreters interpreted you correctly. And if you used a strong word, that's of course you who used it, not anybody else. Is that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that as an answer to a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And what became of him as a result of the leading of the looting exercise?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not under any jurisdiction of mine. I was not able to punish him in any way. And personally, I had never been on good terms with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just listen to the question put to you, Mr. Medakovic. I'm not asking you if you punished him. I'm saying what became of him, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he lived in Plaski. I know that during --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you where he lived, Mr. Medakovic. I said, what became of him? Do you know what became of him as a result of his leading the looting exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can tell, he was responsible to no one and nothing happened to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you who he was responsible to. I'm asking you if you know what became of him.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing happened to him. I saw him after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And don't tell me he was not responsible to anybody, because you have told us that he was a commander of a platoon. He was part of the armed forces. He must be responsible to somebody. Do you know -- or let me put it this way: You said yesterday that you regretted some parts of the letter that you wrote to your counterpart in Ogulin. I can't remember his name. Do you know what became of the forces, the JNA forces, together with the TO and the Special Purpose Unit that attacked Saborsko? Do you know what became of them as a result of the attack on Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That completes my questions. Any questions as a result of the questions by the Bench? Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Moloto ask you whether you knew what became of the JNA units, TO units, and the Special Purpose Unit which took part in the attack on Saborsko. My question to you is as follows: Did the Special Purpose Unit exist and did it take part in the attack on Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated on several occasions that the unit was officially disbanded in September of 1991. I did not wish to point to that in His Honour's question because I was warned on several occasions not to speak about matters that were not asked of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have nothing. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Medakovic, we have come to the conclusion of your testimony. We thank you very much for coming to testify in the Tribunal, and we thank you for the time you took to come and testify. You are now excused. You may stand down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There are a few housekeeping issues that we need to raise before we call the next witness. I'm sorry. I'm not on the microphone. I was just saying there are a few housekeeping issues that we need to raise before we call the next witness, and as I shuffle through my papers to find them, can we start with -- while I'm looking for the issues that I wanted to raise, can we deal with the question of time. At the beginning of this witness's testimony, we were already something like three and a half days behind schedule. This witness in particular had been earmarked to testify for something like five hours in total. It took the Defence 4.05 hours to lead the evidence in chief. It took the Prosecution 8.10 hours to cross-examine him. That must mean that we're falling precipitously behind schedule as we go along. We are just making -- we are not covering the time lost. In fact, we're losing more time. And the Chamber is mindful of the fact that the parties must be given a fair opportunity to present their case, but that being so, the parties are also aware, and the Chamber is aware that we are called upon in terms of the Rules to limit our times and to try and keep as far as we possibly can to the estimates that we have made. I do not think we are succeeding. I do not see how we can hope to cover this time lost unless we sit more sessions per day than are allocated so far. And if it means sitting on a Saturday, we may have to perhaps even think of that. But if we must avoid that, I'd like us to address the question of time. Mr. Milovancevic, you also raised the question of time just before you did your re-examination this morning. Do you want to develop on that? And I would like us to think much -- a little more ahead than go backwards trying to find out how we can cover this time. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the reason why I intervened before re-examination was merely to ask the Trial Chamber to keep in mind the fact that there comes a time when the estimates are simply not feasible because we had to have enough time for the Prosecutor to examine the witness. I'm aware of the situation as you presented it, Your Honour. I am aware of the fact that we are running behind our planned estimate, but I do not think that the situation is quite as drastic as that, because I think that the time has been used most expediently. We had ministers of foreign affairs, ministers of justice, Prime Ministers, chiefs of public security stations as witnesses here. These were relevant witnesses testifying to longer periods of time. As you noticed, the Prosecutor used quite a lot of time examining these witnesses. We are not opposing to that, and we do not wish to criticise the Prosecutor for that fact. Our intention is to fully establish the facts, and if the Prosecutor is contributing to that purpose, then of course I will not criticise that. But I do not wish the Defence to have to bear the consequences of the fact that the Prosecution took longer in their examination than expected. But I do expect that we will have witnesses here who will testify in less time than was set aside for them, because some of their testimony may have been covered by others. This is as much as I have to say on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, it does look as if you're missing my point. I understand what you say, but you yourself started off by saying there comes a time when it's not possible to keep within the estimates. Now, my concern is that it doesn't look like it happens as coming at a time. It seems like it is becoming a pattern. It is a pattern. I said before this witness testified we were already three and a half days behind schedule. So the pattern is growing, and the loss of time is increasing with every witness, and I don't see on the plan where we can get time to cover up this time, and this causes concern. You will remember that I had mentioned to you when you raised it at the beginning of your re-examination that I'd mentioned to you that, yes, I will address this at this point as we are now doing, but I also indicated that the Prosecutor had mentioned, and I think I'm not wrong -- if I'm wrong, I'll be corrected. I think the Prosecutor mentioned at the beginning of this witness's testimony -- or at the beginning of the cross-examination of this witness, that he came up with evidence that had not been supplied in the summary. Now, that causes the problem, you know. If you don't give exhaustive summaries, then we cannot come here and say "We don't want the Prosecution to take the consequences of the Prosecution taking long to cross-examine, because indeed, we didn't give them a full summary." I will ask Mr. Whiting in due course to say what he has to say about this point, but all I'm saying is that the Chamber is concerned about the waste of time. If we take this witness as against five hours that have been estimated, we have used 12 hours. That's more than twice the amount. Now, that is far out of the realm of estimation. You know, if you estimate five hours and you take five and a half hours, the Chamber is not going to gripe about that, but this kind of missing the target is cause for concern. Having said that, Mr. Prosecutor, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First, I'd like to say that I think we have consistently tried to keep our cross-examinations within the time roughly that the direct examination is. Obviously, with this witness it was very different. I would submit -- I don't want to go into it but I would submit that there were very good reasons for it in terms of trying to get answers from the witness. There were a number of interventions from the Trial Chamber itself, and I think that contributed to -- not the interventions, but the fact that it was difficult to get answers to questions, that that contributed to the length. The second thing is another problem that we face is that there are a number of times when the -- when the Defence will cover a rapid series of topics with a witness and will refer to documents without showing the documents to the witness, without going into them. For example, the letter that we had with this witness. There was about a minute of direct examination about the letter, and the letter was not shown to him even though it was listed by the Defence as an exhibit that they would use in their direct examination. It was not shown to him. That's fine. That's their choice. I'm not criticising that. But of course we then feel some obligation to show these documents, talk about them, and that takes some time. So -- so -- and, also, we feel an obligation to cover the topics that have been covered by the Defence. We have an obligation under the Rules to put our case to the witness and to answer those issues. So sometimes those things when they're covered in rapid succession -- for example, I'm not sure why this witness had to talk about events in 1990 and about the chequer-board and we've heard that from witness after witness after witness. But if the witness is going to talk about it, it's our obligation to put our case to the witness. So perhaps there's -- that's one way to save time, would be to focus. But having said that, it's our view that trying to manage the time on a witness per witness basis is a losing proposition for the simple reason is that we think the time estimates that have been given are widely unrealistic and that is the problem. The problem is that the Trial Chamber assessed the Defence case, the nature of the Defence case, came up with a time limit for the Defence case, issued an order about that, and -- and we submit that the Defence should then be left to make their decisions about how that time is going to be used and make their choices about witnesses, picking and choosing witnesses and making decisions if they're going to drop witnesses, if they're going to shorten them, if they're going to emphasise certain ones. That's up to them. Let them do it. Instead, what's happened is the Defence has tried to take this, its original case, and it's trying to shrink it and fit it into the time limits that the Trial Chamber has given, and therefore they have shrunk all the individual estimates of each witness down to unrealistic numbers and so we're caught into this pattern where with each witness we're exceeding those limits, because the limits themselves are not realistic. And really what should happen is the Defence should just make their decisions about how they are going to use their time and what should be firm is the November 20th deadline. That's what's been given to them and the Defence has indicated again and again that they will meet that deadline, that they will not ask for more time. And we submit in the strongest terms, Your Honour, that nothing so far -- there is nothing so far which has provided a basis for extending that deadline because we think the Defence has wasted a lot of time, and that's their choice. That's their decision, but it's a decision they have to live with, and they cannot now come and ask for more time because there has been frankly witness after witness after witness who have testified about cumulative matters, about matters which are not really at issue, about matters that are not necessarily in dispute, and we've had several witnesses who have testified for days on direct examination without even mentioning Milan Martic's name. And the fact that these people may have important titles I do not think is a measure of their relevance to this trial. And so that is really the decision that they -- they have made, and for that reason, we do not think that the Defence has a basis to now come and say, "Well, we're behind schedule. We've had these important witnesses. We need to extend the deadline." No. The deadline is the deadline, and they should -- we should stick to it and let them manage it in that time and let them make the decisions and we'll proceed that way. That is our view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you say, Mr. Whiting, on that point. I just want to ask you a question. You know, my problem -- or the problem of the Chamber, rather, is that it's all very well to say, "You've been given this time, Defence, to present your case. Use your time as you please." And then come the 20th of November, they've called 10 out of 20 witnesses and 10 more witnesses have still not testified. Can it be then said at that stage when you cut them off that they really put their case? I think in short what I'm trying to say to you is the Chamber is trying to balance the question of time with the question of the fair opportunity to present one's case, and I do not think that any Chamber can ever at the end of the Defence case or at the end of the time the Defence is allocated say, "Well, you have 30 more witnesses to call, but I'm sorry, you're not going to call them because you've squandered your time." It would impact very negatively on the fairness of the trial, and this Trial Chamber is trying to make sure that any witness found relevant by any of the parties gets an opportunity to testify, hence the attempt to regulate the time on a witness by witness basis to make sure that they fit in to the time given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand certainly what Your Honour is saying, but I -- I do think that the Trial Chamber can say, "This is the time you have," and the Trial Chamber can cut off the Defence when the time is up unless the Defence can make a compelling showing why another -- one other witness or, you know, two or witnesses needs to be called and was -- and why that witness wasn't called instead of some other witness. And this has been done in other Trial Chambers with both the Prosecution and the Defence. This is not just a Defence issue. This is -- this is -- can be done on both sides. The problem -- the problem the other way, as we see it, is that if that if the Trial Chamber adopts the position that the Defence should be able to call every witness it wants to call, then the time limits will break down and we will continue and this will become unmanageable, because as we can see, the only way to do that is for the Defence to provide witness time limits which are -- which are unrealistic and cannot be met, and they have not been met once I think in this case. Maybe once they have. But with virtually all the witnesses -- I mean, the pattern is clear. And the Defence is in the best position to know who the important witnesses are, how they need to present their case, in what form. If they have decided to spend witness after witness after witness talking about peripheral matters, that is their choice. That is their choice. And if they come at the end of the day and say, "Well, we have 10 more witnesses to call," that unfortunately is too bad. They should have called them. And if they're put on notice now that that is going to be the consequence and those are the choices they have to make, then they are the ones who are in the best position to know and best able to make those choices and make those decisions and make it happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. I don't think it's necessary for us to belabour this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. When it comes to what my learned friend Whiting said, there are matters I agree with and there are others I disagree with and which I consider inappropriate. It is, of course, up to the Defence to decide which witnesses it will call and not the Prosecution. The witnesses we will call will be the witnesses that will benefit our case and not the case of the Prosecution. Of course, it is also up to us to make the time estimates. That is why the statement that we have called witnesses dealing with cumulative matters, peripheral matters simply does not hold. So why does then the Prosecution waste so much time on these so-called peripheral matters? They overstepped every single time limit they had in respect to every witness. So why did the witness yesterday have to talk about the Ustashas for an hour? We've already had this matter discussed. In addition to that, the Bench had numerous questions for our witnesses, and of course we do not find that objectionable. We are quite pleased with that, but this speaks quite to the contrary of what the Prosecutor has been saying. This shows that the witnesses were very much relevant, and it was for that reason that we spent so much time examining these witnesses. That's one matter. The other matter is that the Prosecutor said the time limit is the 20th of November. As far as I know, we haven't asked for the time to be extended, nor do we have that intention. We are quite pleased with the pace of the proceedings. We appreciate the fact that these proceedings bring facts into light. We have a charge involving joint criminal enterprise covering a long time span, and in that context I cannot accept my learned friend's statement that the witness's evidence was cumulative. We are proceeding on the basis of certain time estimates, and we are consuming as much time as we are, but I cannot accept the fact it's been said that we are wasting time on irrelevant on peripheral matters. I believe all the matters we dealt with were very specific. They were not generic, or else we would not be investing as much effort into every single witness's evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't want to go into what the Defence may lead evidence on or may not lead evidence on. That's your choice. And I have my own views as to whether or not the Defence has gone on to cumulative or not, and I'm not expressing that view at all. There was one specific point I wanted to raise with you, to respond to you, Mr. Milovancevic. I can't see it now. Let me say, then, by way of looking forward, I want to suggest specifically to you, Mr. Milovancevic, now that you -- we are in the Defence case, if you can caution your witnesses and control them to be -- to focus on the question and to answer the question put to them. That's the first point. Now, I'm sure you will bear me out that this last witness, and he's not the only one, but it happened many times with him, has been warned by the Bench to please listen to the question and answer that question. And some questions require just a yes or no and then he wants to go into a long story which wastes time. That's one area in which we can try and save time. The other area which we can try and save time is by you putting questions and not prefixing your questions with long dissertations. If you can just put your questions and let's get the answer from the witness and not you first telling a whole long story, at times which contains the answer, and then puts the question. And then you get another story from the witness, and we don't control our witnesses. Otherwise, you're going to force the Bench now to intervene at every question as soon as the witness goes off, the Bench will have to say, "I'm sorry. That's not the question put. That's not the question as put to you." I don't want to do that, particularly when the questions are asked by the parties. I don't want to do that because then the Bench would be taking over the questioning. But I would like you to control your witnesses. And we must control ourselves, too. I think enough said about the subject. I don't want to waste more time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, if I may be allowed to make one point. I would like to direct the Trial Chamber's attention to the fact that the Defence had no difficulties with this witness. All the problems that arose in the examination of the witness were there as a result of the Prosecution's questions or the questions put by the Bench, of course there I can't intervene. That's why I believe the last point you made does not refer to me, or there's nothing that I can do there. If the Prosecutor is the one putting the question, I can have no say in how the witness will answer that question. When I was examining the witness, not a single objection or comment was made to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the matter is you do make long statements before you put the questions, and he did answer questions even by you by making long statements which again do not relate to the question put to him. Yes, I can say, too, that he has done the same also to questions from the Prosecution, and I would ask you, too, Mr. Whiting, as soon as a witness does not answer to your question, stop him. Tell him, "That's not my question." I know you've done it. You haven't done it as much as I would have loved to see. I don't know that you have done it, Mr. Milovancevic, at all. That's why I really addressed myself to you. So again enough said, but I realise that Judge Hoepfel wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, I just wanted to add, Mr. Milovancevic, you will have noticed we interrupted and intervened yesterday during the very extensive, in my view, over-extensive cross-examination, and that was necessary. And I think there was some reason to have a longer cross-examination, but it was not completely justified, I would say. Just for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree with you, Judge Hoepfel. Thank you. That's precisely the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... at this stage, Mr. Milovancevic. Remember also that in terms of economy, the duty is yours in respect of your case. And also part of the preparation process in respect of a witness is to advise him and counsel him as to how to manage his questions and how to answer questions effectively without wasting the Court's time or without being extensive. So it is your specific duty, and you have to always bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And actually, as I understand this system here, it's not only the Court's time, it's your time budget you have to administer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we've said enough. I think that the Chamber is going to have to jump in at every point virtually now, and that might actually cause more delay, but we're going to have to do that if we must save on time. Can I now move on to the next point. The next point really is -- it's not house -- well, it is housekeeping. The next witness is a protected witness and something has to be done and they need more time than usual to do what they have to do to set things up. Unless, therefore, anybody has anything to raise by way of housekeeping, I would suggest that we take the break now and come back at the normal time to give the technicians time to set up for -- in preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's how zealous I am to continue on with the case to cover the lost time. It looks like we can't hear this witness, because they will need more than the time remaining to set up the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's all very well. There are no problems in that regard. If I remember well, we normally adjourn at 1.45, and on behalf of the Defence, I can say that we are not opposed to that. Does that mean that we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, I believe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I answer that question after hearing what Mr. Whiting has to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly have no objection to starting with the next witness tomorrow, but there was -- there were two other matters I needed to raise, and I'm sorry to delay what could have been a welcome early break, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. We are here to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are not here to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The first issue was one that I raised that I hadn't really had an opportunity to address, which was the nature of the 65 ter summaries. I don't know if Your Honours have the summary for this witness handy. I have copies available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry the last witness. The witness who just completed his testimony. And I think it's fair to say that many of the topics which were covered by the witness in direct examination -- do Your Honours need a copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Just to make sure that we have the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I assume the Defence has this available, but there's a copy for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I think it's the same, but just to be on the safe side. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it's fair to say that there were some very important topics that were covered by the witness in direct examination which are not on here. There's nothing about the accused Milan Martic. No mention of him here. And yet that was covered. There's nothing about Golubic. There's nothing about Martic's -- the Special Purpose Unit or the witness's role in the Special Purpose Unit. There's nothing about the Territorial Defence. There is nothing about what happened in the attack in Saborsko. It ends with the action took place on the 12 November 1991. You know, I could go on but I think the point's been made. And the -- I'd like, actually, to also hand out a 65 ter summary of a witness who is upcoming that we -- and -- and this is a witness -- this is Dusan Latas, who we've heard about from this last witness. So we know a little bit about this witness. And there are a couple of things to note. First of all, the 65ter summary for Dusan Latas is nearly on all the relevant points a cut and paste job from the Metkovic 65 ter summary. It's word-for-word the same. That's the first point to notice. The send point is obviously from the testimony that we've heard, we could expect to -- that Mr. Latas would testify about -- about the police and about his role in the attack and what happened, and none of that appears on his 65 ter summary. So I'm foreseeing that this problem is going to occur again. And it's a double problem, Your Honours, because the problem is, first, that of course it makes it very difficult for us to prepare for cross-examination. For example, for this last witness, I was prepared to elicit all that information and I had to completely kind of rework it because then he talked about it, so then I had to deal with it that way. It makes it very difficult and it's unfair. And secondly, it -- this -- not providing us with the information that the witness is going to testify about creates the possibility that future witnesses who come to testify about these events can in some ways consciously or unconsciously mould their testimony to what has occurred before, because obviously we've now had this witness, we've gone through the details, we've put our questions, we've put our case, and the witness coming up, Mr. Latas, could -- again it's the possibility that unconsciously or consciously he could now adjust his testimony to -- to what has occurred, and this is -- this -- I'm a little uncomfortable raising this possibility, but it is frankly an issue that the Tribunal is in the jurisprudence, because for example, when an accused testifies in the Defence case, an accused's testimony will be given more weight if he testifies at the beginning than if he testifies at the end for this very reason. So it is a real possibility, and we think that the weight of the evidence of these Defence witnesses should be affected by the fact that nobody knows what they're going to say about these events until they arrive and they actually say it. They are not in any way committed to anything. There's nothing, and that is in plain breach of the Rules. So that is the concern we raise and we think we should be provided with 65 ter summaries which are accurate and detailed and provide the information on the relevant issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Whiting, I think this question of 65 ter summaries has been -- is some kind of a beaten track by now. We have more than one set of them. Now, I think the solution to this problem should now lie in the hands of the Prosecution. When during leading, a witness is asked questions about issues that are not on the 65 ter summary, I think it should be the responsibility of the Prosecution to jump up and object and say, "That's not on the 65 ter summary. Sorry, you can't lead on it."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that, and we have done that on certain occasions. The difficulty with -- the difficulty here that we faced with this last witness was that I knew that these were matters that I was going to ask him about, because they're obviously part of our case and they're relevant, and so it made -- it puts us in a very difficult position, because I could jump up and say, "Well, you can't talk about that," but then it becomes a little -- well, maybe I could do that and he can't ask any questions about it and I get up and do a cross-examination on those topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. What you do your cross-examination, you are at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's the way we will proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that how trials are conducted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't see any other way because we have asked and asked and asked. And with this last witness we specifically sent an e-mail to the Defence asking -- because we could see that there was going to be more information. It was obvious. We said you must have a supplemental 65 ter. And we got back a few details. I have a copy of the e-mail but, again, nothing about the topics that were covered by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope you hear that, Mr. Milovancevic, and the Trial Chamber is going to be very strict on this one now. If things -- if issues are not raised in the 65 ter summary, I don't think it's fair to allow the Defence to lead that evidence, because then you'd -- it's -- you're taking the Prosecution by surprise, number one. Number two, that's against the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree fully, Your Honours. Yes, I fully agree. My learned friend is right. Before setting out on the field visit, I should have informed him about the detail concerning Golubic. It's my omission. I had no time, because I was preparing for the visit. Mr. Whiting spent 10 minutes on Golubic, and he already had documents about people from Plaski being in that centre, and it was my omission that I didn't know this fact. But we will do whatever we can in the case of future witnesses. And Latas is not in fact the next witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Whoever is next, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Do you want to say something, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, just a short observation now, and I think Judge Nosworthy wanted to add something also. Mr. Milovancevic, I'm really also concerned now realising, for example, the issue of the action against Saborsko on 12th of November, 1991, is being mentioned in both summaries in the very same words, and this is just headings more or less. It's not a summary of the details. It lacks any specificity, I am afraid, so it could cause serious problems for your client. I don't know what to do about that problem, but maybe my colleagues will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And may I just mention, Mr. Milovancevic, that when a statement is said, "Due to the overall situation a decision was reached to free the road," free it from what? We don't know what you're talking about there. I think you've got to be clear what you say in here. Is Saborsko the obstacle on the road? And if Saborsko is the obstacle on the road, why is Saborsko an obstacle on the road? Is it because it's a Croat village and therefore the Croats had to be attacked to be removed from the road? You know, to put it in this kind of euphemistic language, which doesn't really mean much, is not helpful, because then it is not known whether was the road mined and therefore it had to be de-mined, or was the road having some blockades and the blockades had to be removed? You know, I think it's very cryptic, if I may use that term, and I think the summaries leave much to be desired. And I think the only way, as I say, the Chamber is going to have to be very strict on what is on the summary and what is not on the summary. That's the only way that we will be able to get supplemental summaries. Thank you very much. We have come to the end of the day. We are going to take an adjournment, and we will reconvene tomorrow, Friday, the 13th, at 9.00 in courtroom 2, courtroom 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 13th day of October, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
